added_claim_errors: "confirm the office will charge before the 15th": the date the care is provided is what counts, not the date the office charges, so this points the person at the wrong date.

"spending $1,500 on stuff you wouldn't otherwise buy to save $680 is a loss": the math is muddled. On a carryover plan the $680 carries over anyway, and spending protects the $1,220 that would be forfeited, not $680.
"$1,220+ evaporates on January 1": too absolute. Forfeiture is measured at the end of the run-out, and 2026 claims filed during it still count (A does mention the run-out elsewhere).
"Usually ~90 days after Dec 31" for the run-out: a typical figure that varies by plan. It is hedged, so this is minor and unverifiable rather than wrong.

"the carryover only happens if you're still employed and still enrolled in the FSA in the new plan year": stated as a universal rule. The sources leave enrollment as a condition some plans set, so it should be framed as "some plans require it, check yours".

"Health FSA money is use-it-or-lose-it, with only a capped carryover" and the table labeling ~$680 carried over as the "best case": this frames carryover as the only exception, while a grace period (the better outcome for March work) comes up only later as a "nuance".
"Then: spend it before Dec 31, not in March": unconditional advice that ignores the grace-period branch, where March work by the grace end is covered.
"you usually have until March–April to submit receipts": a run-out window that varies by plan. It is hedged, so this is minor and unverifiable.

reasons: Both answers correct the premise at the start, give the right $680 cap and $1,220 forfeiture, say a plan has one feature or neither, and send the person to HR about the run-out. Neither mentions using the 2027 open-enrollment election to pay for the March work. A sets out all three branches (carryover, grace period, neither) up front and gives a plan for each, and it is tighter. It slips on billing timing ("charge before the 15th") and has a muddled $680 remark. B states the service-date rule better ("The service must happen by Dec 31"). But it treats carryover as the main case and the grace period as a nuance, states the enrollment condition as a universal rule, and pushes December spending without regard to branch. It is also longer, with a closing disclaimer. Overall A edges ahead on how it handles the premise, how actionable it is and how concise it is.
